sources.title: 2026 Essential Facts About the U.S. Video Game Industry
sources.method: 20-minute online survey from YouGov's proprietary U.S. panel, weighted by age, gender, ethnicity, education, census region and player status. Household reporting estimates players as young as 5; players 8-17 answered under parental supervision.
caveats: Players are defined as playing at least one hour per week on any platform.
Population estimates are not respondent counts.
Non-binary and prefer not to say are combined and cannot be measured separately.
U.S. players are not a global population or a measure of game-character representation.
Do not interpret the contrast with DiamondLobby's 2017-2021 character sample as change over time.

sources.title: Ready Players All: What Do Gamers Have to Say About Character Diversity?
sources.publisher: Geena Davis Institute / Nielsen Data for Good

sample.population: U.S. and U.K. gamers in Nielsen's weekly Video Game Tracking

caveats: The short report does not state the sample size or a margin of error.
Neither agree nor disagree is calculated as the remainder: 100 minus 62 minus 9.
The 2025 publication reports 2024 fieldwork.
Stated preference is not observed play, purchasing behavior, a causal effect, or a character-representation census.

sources.title: Women in the Workplace 2025
sources.method: Voluntary participating organizations across the U.S. and Canada. Pipeline data reflect 2024 personnel movements, averaged within industries and weighted to Fortune 500 industry composition. A separate third-party employee panel was surveyed in July-August 2025.
caveats: A 2025 publication does not make the pipeline measures 2025 promotions.
Promotion indices compare rates normalized to men at 100; they are not percentages of all promotions.
Women overall includes the displayed subgroups; do not sum overlapping categories.
Sponsor percentages refer to entry-level survey respondents, not all employees.
Observational comparisons do not establish that sponsorship causes promotion.
The voluntary company sample has higher women's representation than typical participating companies in 2021-2024; it is not a census of workplaces.

sources.title: Disability Inclusion @ Work 2024: A Global Outlook
caveats: Full- or part-time employed respondents with disabilities, chronic health conditions or neurodivergence, including people reporting activity difficulties without self-identifying.
Self-reported experiences; not 60% of all workers or of all events.
The photo is illustrative; the people pictured are not identified as respondents.
This is a 2024 study, not a 2026 estimate.

sources.title: Greater Wealth, Greater Uncertainty: Changes in Racial Inequality in the Survey of Consumer Finances
sources.publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

sample.population: U.S. families; survey estimates, not individual-level predictions

caveats: Wealth is assets minus liabilities, not income or personal worth.
Dollar values are in thousands of 2022 dollars, not current nominal dollars.
All five published groups are retained; remaining groups include Native American, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander, other race, and multiple-race families.
2022's oversample first allowed a separate Asian estimate; broad categories hide substantial within-group differences.
The chart shows survey point estimates, not uncertainty intervals. The adjacent arrays retain the source's plus/minus one standard-error endpoints in the same group order.

sources.title: Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025
sources.publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
sources.method: Probability-based Ipsos KnowledgePanel online survey, with post-stratification weights. Cumulative response rate 4.1%. Devices and internet access provided to recruited panel members who needed them.
caveats: A hypothetical $400 emergency, not observed spending.
Cash equivalent includes a credit card paid off at the next statement.
The 37% who would not exclusively use cash are not all unable to pay; payment choice does not establish cash availability.
The 63% and 12% figures are not complementary response categories.
Final analytic sample differs from the number completing the survey.

sources.title: LGBTQ People's Experiences of Workplace Discrimination and Harassment
sources.publisher: Williams Institute, UCLA School of Law
caveats: Self-reported experiences; descriptive group comparisons, not causal estimates.
Past-year discrimination is distinct from harassment, their combined measure, and lifetime experience.
Race and gender comparisons overlap; these are not four mutually exclusive groups or intersection-specific rates.
1,902 is the overall sample, not the size of any subgroup.
Covering refers to behavior at the current job to avoid harassment or discrimination; not every privacy choice is covering.
Higher reported discrimination among out respondents does not establish that disclosure causes discrimination.
Illustrative photographs do not depict identified survey respondents.

sources.title: Inequality in 1,900 Popular Films
sources.publisher: Stacy L. Smith / USC Annenberg Inclusion Initiative
sources.method: Content analysis of 100 top-performing U.S. theatrical films per year; excludes documentaries, television, and music videos. Displayed figures refer to 2025.
caveats: Character shares, creative-role shares, and film-level absence counts have different denominators.
The 2026 publication analyzes 2025 releases, not 2026 films.
Films and identity categories overlap; do not sum absence counts.
Presence counts do not measure depth, quality, agency, stereotypes, or working conditions.
This selected film sample is not a census of all media or a causal study of creative decisions.
Charts redraw published data; publisher graphics and report photography are not reproduced.

sources.title: The WebAIM Million: The 2026 Report

sample.selection: Top home pages derived from the Tranco ranking

sources.method: WAVE automated evaluation of rendered DOMs after scripts and styles.
caveats: Percentages are of tested home pages, not of all websites, errors, or users.
Error categories overlap and must not be summed.
Automated checks detect only some failures. No detected errors does not establish accessibility or WCAG conformance.

sources.title: Systemic Discrimination Among Large U.S. Employers
sources.publisher: Patrick Kline, Evan Rose, Christopher Walters / NBER; Quarterly Journal of Economics
sources.method: Nationwide correspondence experiment randomizing application characteristics and racially associated names at large U.S. employers; NBER working paper first issued July 2021, revised May 2022.
caveats: The randomized effect concerns name signals and employer contact, not a real person's race or job offers.
2.1 percentage points is not a 2.1% relative difference.
The employer effects varied; this is not a current rate for every employer.
The experiment does not identify whether the psychological mechanism is conscious or unconscious bias.
The 2024 Discrimination Report Card grades 97 employers using the underlying experiment; it is not a new experiment with 97 employers.
The slide's two application illustrations summarize the design; qualifications were experimentally varied rather than literally identical across all applications.

sources.title: The Mixed Effects of Online Diversity Training
sources.publisher: Edward H. Chang and colleagues / PNAS
sources.fieldwork: Early 2017 intervention; behavioral follow-up up to 20 weeks
sources.method: Preregistered randomized field experiment among consenting volunteers. Gender-bias training, general-bias training, and active control focused on psychological safety and active listening.
caveats: Attitude and behavioral effects varied by group; do not summarize as either universal success or training never works.
One organization and one brief voluntary intervention do not represent every training program.
Learn, rehearse, change the process, and check impact is a teaching suggestion, not a tested intervention package.
The captioned-call illustration is not a depiction of the study or its participants.

sources.title: Six Actions to Create Genuine DEI Policies
sources.publisher: Kathrina Robotham, Danielle Jackson, Tara Van Bommel / Catalyst

sample.population: Full-time employees recruited through a panel service

sources.method: Online survey and observational regression analyses of organizational characteristics and perceived policy genuineness.
caveats: Associations, not a randomized evaluation of interventions.
The .52 R-squared is explained variance, not 52% of employees or a success rate.
Room to speak condenses preventing a climate of silence in the teaching diagram.
The ownership and feedback checklist is a teaching application, not a validated score or guaranteed outcome.

sources.title: The 5Ds of Bystander Intervention
caveats: A practical framework, not an effect-size estimate or a sequential escalation ladder.
Assess safety and follow the person harmed; direct confrontation is not always appropriate.
Before documenting, ensure someone is helping and assess safety. Never publish or use documentation without permission.
Delegation must consider the person's wishes; do not assume police involvement is wanted.
